title: A systemic C balance to evaluate the environmental role of productive systems
author: Biagini

steps.title: Define system boundaries
steps.instruction: Specify which processes and stages belong to the system and which are excluded. For a specialised growing‑finishing cattle operation include only the fattening process; for a whole‑cycle livestock farm include animal, plant and energy production and transformation of raw products; a consortium of farms may be treated as a single system.

steps.title: Identify processes and links
steps.instruction: List every productive process (e.g., animal grazing on permanent grasslands, cultivation of feed crops, market crops, non‑harvested species such as bees, wood production, other land uses, animal reproduction, animal fattening, raw‑product transformation, energy production) and note how the output of each (products, by‑products, wastes) serves as input to another process, whether the material exchange is explicit or implicit.

steps.title: Draw flowchart of connections
steps.instruction: Create a graphic representation of the relationships identified in step 2 using boxes for stocking sites and arrows for material fluxes (solid for external inputs, broken for external outputs, dotted for internal fluxes).

steps.title: Gather raw farm data
steps.instruction: Measure, estimate, calculate or retrieve from official documents all data required to quantify material flows, then verify them during site visits. Required data include: farm surface use, cultivated species, field areas, average crop and wood yields, productive factors (self‑produced or purchased), cultivation operations, sold productions, animal categories and numbers, average live weight, diet composition, dry‑matter intake, average parities per cow per year, calving interval, average milk per cow per year and its fat/protein contents, growth rates, numbers/ages/weights of animals slaughtered per year, and energy sources and consumptions.

steps.title: Aggregate homogeneous data
steps.instruction: Combine comparable data from different productive processes to simplify later calculations, e.g., sum weight gain of fattening and breeding animals or add crop/grassland areas of all consortium units.

steps.title: Compute derived variables and ranges
steps.instruction: Use mathematical models, formulas, coefficients or literature values to derive variables such as plant net C exchange, crop residues, animal body composition, respiratory gas exchange, enteric gas production, faeces and urine excretion, manure spreading, fuel consumption, dissolved organic C, organic‑matter oxidation/reduction and methane oxidation. Estimate the most probable range of variation for each variable from bibliographic references or from sensitivity knowledge obtained during data collection. For enteric gases, calculate them as C input (feed) minus C retained (average weight gain) minus C outputs (milk, calves, respiration, faeces, urine), which is more complete than direct measurements that often detect only methane (e.g., SF₆ tracer or open‑path laser).

steps.title: Transform fluxes to carbon equivalents
steps.instruction: Convert all material and energy fluxes to equivalent carbon weight using stoichiometric conversion coefficients: 0.27291 for CO₂, 0.74882 for CH₄, 0.19998 for CH₄N₂O (urea), 0.46 for protein, 0.70 for fats, 0.40 for carbohydrates (CₙH₂ₙOₙ), 0.36 for urine, 0.50 for plants or plant‑derived products (based on average formula CH₁.₄₄O₀.₆₆), 0.15–0.20 for live weight (breed‑specific), and 723.2 g L⁻¹ for oil. For carbon per kWh of electricity, refer to the national CO₂‑emission inventory for the local energy mix.

steps.title: Classify carbon fluxes
steps.instruction: Assign each carbon flux to one of three categories: Input (purchased seeds, plants, fertilizers, pesticides, medicines, feeds, litter, animals, fuel, net plant exchange from air), Output (sold animal or plant products, soil C redox, dissolved organic C, gases from manure storage, enteric gases, respiratory gases, fuel‑combustion gases, electricity consumption), or Internal (reused streams such as straw, manure, self‑produced feeds, replacement animals, milk, crop residues).

steps.title: Calculate net carbon balance
steps.instruction: Sum all input fluxes with a positive sign and all output fluxes with a negative sign; the net carbon balance equals Σ(inputs) + Σ(outputs). Example expression: plant growth (+) + purchased feeds (+) + fuel (+) + fertilizers, pesticides, medicines (+) + soil losses (‑) + animal respiration (‑) + enteric fermentation (‑) + sold animals/products (‑) + sold plant products (‑) + fuel combustion (‑) + electricity use (‑) = net C balance.

steps.title: Interpret and analyse results
steps.instruction: Relate the net carbon change to one or more functional units (e.g., ha, tonnes of live weight slaughtered, tonnes of milk) and compute derived indexes: carbon efficiency = net balance ÷ total inputs; intensity = inputs per functional unit. Perform a sensitivity analysis using the estimated variation ranges for inputs and outputs (±10 % after rounding the original ±10.4 % and ±9.9 %). Determine whether the system is a carbon sink (positive balance), source (negative) or neutral (zero).
